@raulsntos Will this and other Godot C# full features run smoother in the long run as Godot 5.x? As in developing if Godot 4.x gets prototype C# features (such as web support) running and then in Godot 5.x it is optimized with the 'would be nice' features like size and security optimizations? I say this after reading your and the creative community's comments on the C# suite features and the prototype type work and potential for better solutions ( https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/70796#issuecomment-2860126678 ). 

<details>
I wonder this in order to better plan big projects (like a working vertical slice C# MIT Smooth Voxel MMORPG template for Godot) be it Godot 4.x and or Godot 5.x due to API and other complex team coordination which requires a stable software platform / game engine to first under take. If a Godot 5.x alpha with C# full features is being built soon (Godot 4.x may already be past its mid-life cycle once 4.5 is stable) it might be better for the 'power users' / big movers / proper game studios of the creative community to 'Wait for Godot' than to force teams of people to re-engine from Godot 4.x to Godot 5.x. Software long term stability is very critical for long term planning. 

A lot of senior game studios are re-engining now and it is by default UE5 but personally I'd like it to be Godot also. A lot of studios are re-engining from the Unity implosion and I want Godot to succeed where Unity failed. Yet long term stability is very critical for the old grumblers of the industry.

Thus starting on a prototype Godot 5.x alpha with full C# features and optimizations and long term stability (and other details that require stability like Godot C# API issues being fully addressed) after ~Godot 4.5 stable is probably a practical way forward for the Godot creative community to keep both near future growth of Godot game engine progressing well and also keep Godot 4.x stable. Godot should get ready for the next gaming generation come 2027 / the late 2020's. Official Godot 5.x alpha plans for a feature roadmap can do a lot to also powerfully grow and future proof the Godot game engine creative community for today's and tomorrow's game building adventures.

It seems like Godot 4.x will get unified C# support as a GDextension and full C# parity support; yet this might be as prototype form. Once the Godot 4.x full C# features are operational this whole suite of C# features might require optimizations that are only properly done with seeing everything on the table first in working form and then in a big strong unified effort lead a proper engine rewrite to properly integrate the features to be optimized for being the best they can be. As from what can be currently done as the creative community for this console generation and the next console / gaming generation planned for 2027 / late 2020's with the PS6 / new Xbox / next gen consoles and gaming hardware.

The work of https://github.com/raulsntos and friends is very helpful to the creative community and I wish to thank the people involved greatly. This kind of work helps the creative community to make great games for everyone.
</details>

> Hey @MadBunnyGames - is there any chance you would be willing to share how you got the .net build working?

Basically pulled the changes from here into a 4.4.1 (or some nightly 4.5 dev, not sure), edited the .csproj file to match .net version and threading support, built the editor and the templates (as Godot documentation says... note: I use windows and had to switch to WSL when building the web template, because emscc command was too long for PowerShell), also set up a local nuget store for godot package during build (its in godot docs too), matched my project file, referenced the newly built nugets, needed to add entrypoint to the project (main function), then built and exported the project with the new templates, manually removed the DOTNET.setup(...) call from the .js that was generated for the c# project, then just uploaded to itch as is. 
Had some road bumps along the way, but I don't really remember them, because it was 2+ months ago.

If you want to try out the solution made by @raulsntos and reproduced by @MadBunnyGames and you aware how to use Docker you could try my "one liner" to achieve the web build. Nothing is guaranteed, it's all experimental and may break.
I’ve created a Docker image to streamline the HTML5 export process for Godot .NET projects using Godot 4.5. You can run it with the following command in your project folder:
`docker container run --rm -v ".:/src" kstgrd/godot-mono-web:4.5.dev`
This will generate a `build` directory with the exported project and an index.zip file ready for upload to itch.io. As a proof of concept, I’ve successfully built and uploaded a prototype here: https://kstgrd.itch.io/godot45net?secret=lc3VjeGNpn4PXlzJZRattN79s


P.S. ~4gb will be downloaded by docker to get the image
Update:
- demo project source: [here](https://github.com/xr0gu3/net-web-example)
- your `.csproj` should use `<TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>` as image was built relying on that version of .NET
- don't forget to create an empty Program.cs file in your project root with an empty public static void Main() function in it
```csharp
public class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        
    }
}
```

Hey @AR-DEV-1 I've tried a lot of things, and I will share with you:

## About incompatibility with `4.5`/`4.5.1`:
Apparently this preview works fine with `4.5.1` if you doesn't use multithreading. Like you can use `new Thread()` by example, but any heavy execution will crash the game and the page, you can see it in the @raulsntos prototype, if you export with Threads supports but add `WithConcurrentBuild(false)` in the code compilation you will se everything works. 

In my case I tested with my personal project which is using exactly this PR and enabling multithreads.

With this preview (`4.4` + web support) everything works fine, multithreading or not, my project only uses `.ConfigureAwait(false)` in many places.

With this preview + `4.5.1-stable` the game crashes in the first `ConfigureAwait(false)`.

What I've tried to fix:

- Set Max and Min ThreadPool in the C# side:

```cs
// Both calls returned true, also checked with ThreadPool.GetMaxThreads
ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(1, 1);
ThreadPool.SetMaxThreads(6, 1);
```

- Changed `Godot Pool Size` to **6** and **8**.
- Disabled Godot Wasm SIMD with: `scons platform=web target=template_debug threads=yes dev_build=yes dev_mode=true module_mono_enabled=true wasm_simd=false`

Yeah nothing fixed it, I really don't know what really change between `4.4` and `4.5` to break the multithreading in .NET side.

## About the stubs, the "Js Problem"
Yeah this will be hard to fix I reflected and studied a lot about the Interop with JS in .NET Wasm and the only solution I consider will be this:

- Every `[JsImport]` will use a source generator to generate a call to the JS side, they will invoke [these functions](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/v9.0.10/src/libraries/Common/src/Interop/Browser/Interop.Runtime.cs).
- It will use `libSystem.Native` which communicate with `dotnet.runtime.js` [C# Class Ref](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/v9.0.10/src/libraries/Common/src/Interop/Browser/Interop.Libraries.cs), [Doc Ref](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/tree/626ad3211336cee8d8e805580d060fd60d24f207/src/native/corehost/browserhost)
- With this maybe we can wrap the call? For me it's a bad solution but maybe it's a start, I also will add some interesting files about these calls: [corebindings.c](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/626ad3211336cee8d8e805580d060fd60d24f207/src/mono/browser/runtime/corebindings.c#L49), [JsFunctionBinding (called by source generators)](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/626ad3211336cee8d8e805580d060fd60d24f207/src/libraries/System.Runtime.InteropServices.JavaScript/src/System/Runtime/InteropServices/JavaScript/JSFunctionBinding.cs#L372), [JS Side](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/626ad3211336cee8d8e805580d060fd60d24f207/src/mono/browser/runtime/invoke-js.ts#L36).

## Finishing...

I've checked, .NET 10 changed some things about the .wasm export and maybe it will help us (or it will blow everything, who knows)

## What changed?
So... 

- `pinvoke-table.h` disappeared.
- `wasm_m2n_invoke.g.h` disappeared too.
- Now `dotnet.native.js` and `dotnet.runtime.js` are exported separetely.

## What I've done?

I've figure out how make the templates works with .NET 10, but when I export my app it fails unfortunately:

- Change `TargetFramework` `net9.0` to `net10.0` in `GetRuntimePack.csproj`
- Add the tags `<IsBrowserWasmProject>true</IsBrowserWasmProject>` and `<WasmGenerateAppBundle>false</WasmGenerateAppBundle>` in PropertyGroup browser-wasm, also in `GetRuntimePack.csproj`. This make `pinvoke-table.h` and `wasm_m2n_invoke.g.h`  be generated again.
- Replace `get_runtime_pack_project_includes` `net9.0` to `net10.0` in `mono_configure.py`.

- `__099ced52:0xaa0ef4__ Uncaught (in promise) RuntimeError: function signature mismatch`

So probably the stubs in `ManagedCallbacks` aren't matching with the `pinvoke-table.h`.

Hi Raul. I've been working on C# Web export and ended up on the same architecture as this PR: Mono embedding APIs statically linked, a `GetRuntimePack` helper to resolve the runtime pack, `PInvokeTableGenerator` feeding `pinvoke-table.h`. I found your PR after the fact, which is a little awkward, but the overlap is close enough that I'd rather bring the work here than open something separate and pretend it's unrelated.

Branch: https://github.com/jlucaso1/godot/pull/1

The three things this PR lists as open are working there.

**Globalization.** ICU is linked into the template and its data is loaded from the published payload, so invariant mode isn't forced anymore. `Interop/JsGlobalization::GetLocaleInfo` is implemented on the engine side. Cultures, collation, Turkish casing and `NativeName`/`DisplayName` all behave.

**The JavaScript stubs.** Rather than patching `dotnet.runtime.js`, the engine supplies those imports itself through a `godot_mono_glue.js` linked into the template. That covers the jiterpreter entry points, browser entropy (so crypto works), the globalization and timezone queries, and the single threaded `[JSImport]` binding path.

**Manual edits to the exported `.js`.** Not needed. Export produces a game that runs.

Two places I ended up differing from this PR, and both are worth your opinion rather than me just asserting I got it right.

**Trimming.** I couldn't keep it on. `Microsoft.NET.ILLink.targets` always roots the project's own assembly in `EntryPoint` mode, and making the game a library (which is what lets the engine be the host and skip relinking) leaves it without one, so publish fails with IL1034 no matter what roots you add beside it. So trimming and per project relinking look like one decision to me rather than two: keep relinking and you can trim, drop it and you can't, but then nobody exporting a game needs emscripten on their machine. I went the second way. The payload cost is real and I'd rather that trade were made deliberately than inherited from me.

**How the interop closure gets enumerated.** I pointed the generator at the real `GodotSharp.dll` and `GodotPlugins.dll` instead of a hand written `ManagedCallbacks.cs`. It costs a heavier build order, since an editor and the managed assemblies have to exist first, but the numbers were larger than I expected: the generated table carries 148 interpreter entry points against 37 in the checked in stub file. The rest only fail once something reaches them, which may account for some of the rough edges here.

There's also a CI job that builds the whole chain from a fresh checkout and then exports a project and runs it in headless Chromium, asserting on what the game prints. That's how the two worst bugs on my side surfaced: a wasm32 struct return ABI mismatch that trapped the browser on `Variant.ToString()`, and a `[JSImport]` exception path that had never worked, returning the right message text followed by megabytes of adjacent heap while still arriving with the right exception type.

Happy to do whatever is most useful with this. I can split it into pieces against this PR, hand over individual parts, or just leave it here as a reference. Worth noting that my branch is on current master and this one is from May 2025, so merging in either direction probably means rebasing this PR forward first.

Disclosure, since Godot asks for it: this was written with Claude Code working under my direction and codex reviewing every commit. Thanks for your hard work

Hi Raul - I explored the missing JavaScript-interop part of this PR, specifically how to remove the manual exported-JS edits without initializing Mono twice.

The original spike treated Godot as the runtime owner (mono_wasm_load_runtime remains in Godot) and used the matching runtime pack's dotnet.runtime.js only to replace the linker placeholders and initialize the JS marshalers. That would require a very small, explicit embedding surface in dotnet/runtime, rather than running the normal .NET startup sequence.

However, the situation has moved on since that spike was prepared. The recent work in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/118976/https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/121871 and https://github.com/jlucaso1/godot/pull/1 demonstrates Godot-side/static-LibGodot approaches, and the latest comment here reports working Godot-side imports, crypto, globalization, [JSImport], no manual export edits, and end-to-end browser CI. Given that evidence, I don't want to advocate for an upstream runtime hook if the Godot-side closure is the preferred direction.

I investigated the remaining JS interop blocker in #106125, specifically the `runtime_idx` stubs generated by `dotnet.es6.lib.js`.

The useful split seems to be:

1. Godot keeps ownership of WASM instantiation and native Mono startup (`mono_wasm_load_runtime`).
2. The .NET browser runtime is used only for its JavaScript interop layer.
3. Before Godot's `WebAssembly.instantiate*`, the host needs the equivalent of .NET's private `replace_linker_placeholders(imports)`.
4. After Godot has called `mono_wasm_load_runtime`, the host needs the JS-side equivalent of `init_c_exports()` + `cwraps_internal(INTERNAL)` + `bindings_init()`, but **without** starting Mono a second time.

`dotnet.runtime.js` currently exports `setRuntimeGlobals`, `initializeExports`, `initializeReplacements`, `passEmscriptenInternals`, and the normal startup functions, but it does not export those two embedding phases. The normal `configureEmscriptenStartup()` is not suitable here because the .NET startup path also owns runtime initialization.

I have a local spike that keeps `dotnet.runtime.js` unmodified and would only require two internal upstream hooks, conceptually:

```ts
replaceLinkerPlaceholdersForEmbedding(imports)
initializeInteropForEmbedding()
```

Godot's already-linked `DOTNET.setup()` can still provide the real `wasmMemory`, `wasmTable`, and `updateMemoryViews` closures through `passEmscriptenInternals`; the Godot adapter only replaces `configureEmscriptenStartup` with an import-patching wrapper. After the C++ `mono_wasm_load_runtime()` call, a tiny Emscripten JS-library callback initializes the JS interop layer.

This should avoid the brittle approach of editing/minified `dotnet.runtime.js` while preserving Godot as the owner of Mono startup.
